name: The Faith
label: Dischord
lede: Two years, one side of an LP and an eight-song EP, and the band a lot of D.C. kids felt closer to than Minor Threat.

eras.title: Filling the quiet
eras.text: By fall 1981 several D.C. bands had broken up at once and the scene went briefly fallow. Two S.O.A. veterans, the Untouchables' singer and a bass player from Wilson High stepped into the gap, and inside a few weeks of their first show they were opening for Bad Brains at CBGB.

years.h: Out of S.O.A. and the Untouchables
years.p: [[Michael Hampton|4ed83c42-6348-4368-903e-9116bfa49b8e]] and [[Ivor Hanson|a17981f7-ab3d-46dc-859a-582ac894cb20]] come over from [[State of Alert|e54cb250-3502-4c32-9482-70488bd9a8cb]], [[Alec MacKaye|bb05a948-ea44-4c9b-9d19-2a48f757ca22]] from the Untouchables, and fellow Wilson High kid [[Chris Bald|0838359b-95a7-48e9-a9f6-0e8f40bb34d2]] picks up the bass. Alec is [[Ian MacKaye|c12f644b-1066-4ead-b0dd-d0c380f5cca2]]'s younger brother.

years.cap: Alec MacKaye and Michael Hampton at the Chancery, Washington, D.C., 1981.
years.h: First show: a high school in Arlington
years.p: The Faith debut at H.B. Woodlawn High School. Before the year is out they're also playing the Chancery in D.C.

[[Ian MacKaye|c12f644b-1066-4ead-b0dd-d0c380f5cca2]] produces the band's first demo in Arlington. Nearly every song will be re-recorded for the split LP; the demo itself stays unreleased for 30 years.

years.cap: Recorded at CBGB, December 1981, and released later by Outer Battery.
years.p: A few weeks after their first show, the Faith are on the Bowery opening for Bad Brains. Someone rolls tape, and the set later comes out as Live at CBGB's on Outer Battery.

eras.title: Their side of the record
eras.text: The Faith spent 1982 getting onto vinyl and getting bigger. Dischord paired them with Void for a split LP, and the band added a second guitarist to fill out a sound that was already changing.

years.p: Twelve Faith songs on one side, [[Void|960a1d2f-2b5f-4fcf-bf11-4957529a6508]] on the other, recorded at Inner Ear with production credited to Ian, Jeff, Don, Bert and the band. The first pressing sells out in two weeks.
years.xp:
The Washington Post later described the Faith as taking the snarl of British punk, speeding it up and making it distinctly American. Next to Void's glorious wreck of a side, the Faith side is taut and pointed.

The record found fans far from D.C. Kurt Cobain put it in his top 50 albums of all time, and Thurston Moore called it the most potent distillation of early D.C. straight edge hardcore.

years.h: A second guitar from the Untouchables
years.p: [[Eddie Janney|323dd1dd-23e4-45ce-9aa9-c5492096d604]], Alec's old Untouchables bandmate, joins alongside Hampton. The Faith are now a five-piece.

eras.title: Stopping at the top
eras.text: The five-piece Faith wrote longer, more thoughtful songs, and then decided they were done. Their last record came out after their last show, which is part of why it hit people so hard.

q: It was a good time to stop.
years.src: Washington City Paper · Dischord Records · Wikipedia
years.p: The Faith play their final show as headliners, about two years after their debut. The fans weren't ready.
years.xp:
No single reason for the split is on the record. Hampton, looking back decades later, simply thought the timing was right.

The audience felt otherwise. Dischord's own bio says that while [[Minor Threat|09037f07-42bc-46ac-a1ee-37f834451fee]] gets held up as the defining D.C. band of those years, for many people who lived there it was the Faith they connected with most. [[Ian MacKaye|c12f644b-1066-4ead-b0dd-d0c380f5cca2]] remembered how unhappy people were.

years.src: Dischord Records · Wikipedia · Washington City Paper
years.p: Eight songs, about thirteen minutes, on a 12-inch EP, produced by [[Ian MacKaye|c12f644b-1066-4ead-b0dd-d0c380f5cca2]] and the band at Inner Ear. It comes out roughly four months after the last show, so most listeners meet the five-piece Faith after it's gone.
years.xp:
It's the only record of the five-piece Faith, with Janney's guitar alongside Hampton's.

The fans who missed it live took it hard. [[Ian MacKaye|c12f644b-1066-4ead-b0dd-d0c380f5cca2]] summed up the reaction years later.

eras.title: Everybody starts the next band
eras.text: The Faith's five members fanned out across the next wave of D.C. music. Follow almost any branch of mid-80s Dischord back far enough and you hit one of them.

years.p: Janney co-founds the band with [[Guy Picciotto|f8200cea-b5e9-4145-b5a5-1d0838f2c288]], part of the wave that follows hardcore in D.C.

years.h: Three Faith members and Ian MacKaye form [[Embrace|9d1ad8e3-8740-429a-bdc5-52f96a9c4431]]
years.p: Hampton, Bald and Hanson back [[Ian MacKaye|c12f644b-1066-4ead-b0dd-d0c380f5cca2]], who has moved on from [[Minor Threat|09037f07-42bc-46ac-a1ee-37f834451fee]]. The older brother ends up singing in front of his younger brother's band.

years.h: Janney and Hampton in One Last Wish
years.p: The two Faith guitarists reunite in [[One Last Wish|94f18045-7fe2-41df-bf24-0bed21c88eb8]], which later becomes [[Happy Go Licky|4c18be5e-2e53-41a4-a4a1-d9080ff88f8c]]. Alec MacKaye and Chris Bald, meanwhile, go on to form [[Ignition|3cb2b7d6-1f0b-4ac5-b67f-52132f3d3b61]].

years.h: Hampton and Hanson again, in Manifesto
years.p: The partnership that ran through S.O.A., the Faith and Embrace, now ten years old, picks up one more time.

eras.title: Renewed Faith
eras.text: Nearly thirty years on, Dischord went back to the Faith's tapes. The 2011 reissue finally put the band's first recordings next to its last and sent a new round of writers back to the split.

years.p: The Faith take their place on the label's anniversary box set.

years.h: Subject to Change plus First Demo · Dischord No. 172
years.p: The EP, remastered from the original tapes, plus the eleven-song December 1981 demo, unreleased until now. It's the first time Subject to Change has been on vinyl since 1988, this time on clear vinyl.
play: Subject to Change plus First Demo

years.h: The split gets its due, again
years.p: In The Guardian, [[The Hold Steady|4883523d-fc0e-4d0d-802c-91379e767083]]'s Craig Finn calls Faith/Void one of the most vital hardcore records ever released.
